DRY LAB
             (Week 3)




      OBJECTIVES

1. Define the boundaries and divisions of the
mediastinum (superior, anterior, middle,
posterior).
2. Identify the structures within the superior
mediastinum (trachea, esophagus, brachiocephalic
veins, SVC, aortic arch and its branches).
3. Identify the branches of the aortic arch:
brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery,
left subclavian artery.
4. Locate the vagus and phrenic nerves within the
superior and middle mediastinum.
5. Identify the contents of the anterior
mediastinum.
6. Identify the contents of the middle mediastinum
(heart, pericardium, ascending aorta, pulmonary
trunk, SVC, IVC, pulmonary veins).
7. Identify the structures in the posterior
mediastinum (descending thoracic aorta,
esophagus, azygos venous system, thoracic duct,
sympathetic trunks).

8. Differentiate between the azygos, hemiazygos, and
accessory hemiazygos veins.
9. Identify the ligamentum arteriosum and the relation of the
left recurrent laryngeal nerve to the arch of the aorta and
explain the relevance to patent ductus arteriosus and to
hoarseness.
10. Identify the thoracic sympathetic trunk, its ganglia, and the
greater and lesser splanchnic nerves.

MEDIASTINUM

1.Mediastinum





       Anterior                    Sternum

        Posterior                   Vertebral column

       Superior              Superior thoracic aperture

         Inferior                   Diaphragm

        Lateral                   Mediastinal pleura

B. Divisions

The mediastinum is divided into superior and
inferior mediastinum.
A transverse plane from the sternal angle to the
T4/T5 intervertebral disc separates the superior
mediastinum from the inferior mediastinum.
The inferior mediastinum is divided into three
compartments:
  1.Anterior mediastinum
 2.Middle mediastinum
 3.Posterior mediastinum

C. Contents of the Mediastinum

 Superior Mediastinum
   Thymus (or remnants)
    Brachiocephalic veins / SVC
    Aortic arch and branches
    Trachea
   Oesophagus
    Thoracic duct
   Vagus and phrenic nerves
 Anterior Mediastinum
    Loose connective tissue and fat
   Lymph nodes
    Sternopericardial ligaments
    Internal thoracic vessels
   Thymus/remnants
 Middle Mediastinum
    Heart and pericardium
    Ascending aorta
   Pulmonary trunk
   SVC/IVC
   Pulmonary veins
    Phrenic nerves
    Tracheal bifurcation
   Main bronchi and tracheobronchial nodes
 Posterior Mediastinum
    Descending thoracic aorta
   Oesophagus
   Azygos system
    Thoracic duct
   Vagus nerves
    Sympathetic trunks
    Splanchnic nerves
    Posterior mediastinal nodes

D. Aortic Arch Branches (Right to Left)
              →
    Brachiocephalic trunk   right common carotid
   and right subclavian arteries.
    Left common carotid artery.
    Left subclavian artery.

E. Nerves and Key Relations

1. Phrenic nerves
   Descend anterior to the roots of the lungs,
   between mediastinal pleura and pericardium.
   Motor supply to diaphragm.
2. Vagus nerves
   Pass posterior to the roots of the lungs.
   Contribute to the oesophageal plexus.
3. Left recurrent laryngeal nerve
   Loops under the aortic arch beside the
   ligamentum arteriosum, then ascends toward
   the larynx.
   Compression can cause hoarseness.
4. Ligamentum arteriosum
   Ligamentum arteriosum is the adult remnant of
   the ductus arteriosus, connecting the left
   pulmonary artery region to the aortic arch.
   Persistent patency is patent ductus arteriosus
   (PDA).

F. Azygos Venous System

1. Azygos vein
- Mainly drains the right posterior thoracic wall
and empties into the SVC.
2. Hemiazygos vein
- Drains lower left posterior intercostal spaces and
crosses to join the azygos vein.
3. Accessory hemiazygos vein
- Drains upper/middle left posterior intercostal
spaces and crosses to the azygos vein.
4. Thoracic sympathetic trunk and splanchnic
nerves
   Thoracic sympathetic trunk lies
   paravertebrally.
   Thoracic splanchnic nerves arise from it and
   carry mainly sympathetic fibres to abdominal
   viscera.

WET LAB




 OBJECTIVES

NOSE
  The Nasal Cavity

Basic Layout
The nose has 2 cavities (left and right), each with a lateral
(side) wall. The two cavities are divided in the middle by the
nasal septum.
Conchae & Meatus
Each lateral wall has folds that stick into the cavity. These folds
are the conchae (also called turbinates), and there are 3 on
each side. The grooves or empty spaces tucked underneath
each fold are the meatus.
Conchae: superior, middle , inferior
•   Meatus: superior, middle, inferior (each one sits below its
matching concha)

Sphenoethmoidal Recess
Above the superior concha is the sphenoethmoidal recess. It
sits between the base of the skull and the superior concha. This
is where the sphenoid sinus drains into the nasal cavity.

Superior meatus
•   Opening for the posterior ethmoidal sinus
Middle meatus (the busiest one)
•   Bulla ethmoidalis: the middle ethmoidal sinus opens on it
•   Hiatus semilunaris: a curved groove just below the bulla.
The maxillary sinus opens here
•   Infundibulum: a channel leading up to the frontal sinus.
The anterior ethmoidal sinus also drains here
Inferior meatus
•   Opening of the nasolacrimal duct
Tears and the Runny Nose
Tears collect in the lacrimal lake, then drain through the
lacrimal canaliculi into the lacrimal sac, then down the
nasolacrimal duct into the inferior meatus.
That is why crying makes your nose run. There is a lot of fluid
and no time for the tears to evaporate, so you end up blowing
your nose.
The Floor
The floor (base) of the nasal cavity is the hard palate.

2. Choana & Nasopharynx

  Choana
  The choana is the opening at the back of the nasal cavity. It
  has no door, and it connects the nasal cavity to the
  nasopharynx. It sits just behind the posterior border of the
  palatine bone.
  Borders of the choana:
  •   Medial (midline): vomer
  •   Inferior: horizontal plate of the palatine bone
  •   Lateral: medial pterygoid plate of the sphenoid
  •   Superior: ala of the vomer + vaginal process of the medial
  pterygoid plate + body of the sphenoid
  Nasopharynx
  The nasopharynx is the part of the pharynx behind the nasal
   cavity. It runs from the skull base down to the level of the soft
  palate.

•   At the junction of the roof and the posterior wall sits the
adenoid (pharyngeal tonsil)
•   The lateral wall has an opening for the Eustachian
(auditory) tube, connecting to the middle ear
•  A raised bump, the torus tubarius, sits right on top of the
tubal opening, with a small pocket (the pharyngeal recess) just
behind it
•   The roof also has a normal shallow depression that is not
related to the Eustachian tube

3. Oropharynx &
   Laryngopharynx

Oropharynx
Starts below the level of the hard and soft palate and runs
down to the upper border of the epiglottis. It sits at vertebral
levels C2 to C3.
•   Palatine tonsils are found here, in the upper part
Laryngopharynx
Starts where the oropharynx ends, at the epiglottis, and runs
down to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage (the lamina
of the cricoid). It sits at vertebral levels C4 to C6.
•     It continues below as the oesophagus (not the trachea; the
trachea is the airway that begins in front of it)

4. The Nasal Septum

Sagittal vs Midsagittal Section
•   Sagittal cut (off to the side): you see the lateral wall with
its folds, the conchae
•   Midsagittal cut (right down the middle): you see the
smooth septum
What the Septum Is Made Of
•   Anterior part: cartilage (septal cartilage)
•   Posterior and upward: bone (perpendicular plate of the
ethmoid), with the vomer at the back and below
Kiesselbach's Area & Nosebleeds
The cartilaginous part of the septum has a spot called
Kiesselbach's area (or Little's area). It is where several arteries
anastomose (join up), which makes it very vulnerable and the
most common site of epistaxis (nosebleed).
Blood supply of the septum comes from:
•   Facial artery (superior labial branch), entering from the
front
•   Greater palatine artery, from below (the inferior border)
•   Sphenopalatine artery, from behind (posteriorly)
•   Anterior ethmoidal artery, from above. The posterior
ethmoidal artery supplies the upper septum too

LARYNX
      1. THE BASIC IDEA


•  Lets assume, larynx as an hourglass and go from base to
top.
•  Bottom end is cartilage, top end is cartilage, and the cords
sit in the narrow middle.
•  The top half is more or less a mirror copy of the bottom
half, so if you know one side the other is easy.
              →
•  Matching pairs (bottom   top):
          →
-  cartilage: cricoid   epiglottis cartilage
                           →
- membrane: cricovocal membrane (dome shaped)
quadrangular membrane
             →
-  cords: true vocal cords   false vocal cords

2. BOTTOM HALF



CRICOID CARTILAGE
•  Sits at the base. Shape is a ring.
•  Only complete circular cartilage in the larynx.
•  Below the cricoid is the trachea.
CRICOVOCAL MEMBRANE
•  Comes straight after the cricoid, shaped like a dome.
•  The edge of the opening at the top of the dome is the vocal
cord (the vocal ligament).
•  Vocal cords attach at the front to the inner angle of the
thyroid cartilage, and at the back to the arytenoids (vocal
process).

3. TOP HALF



•  Cords: false vocal cords, also called vestibular cords.
•  Membrane: quadrangular membrane.
•  Cartilage: epiglottis cartilage.
• Same pattern as the bottom, just flipped. The false cords
are the lower free edge of the quadrangular membrane, the
same way the true cords are the free edge of the cricovocal
one.

4. GLOTTIS AND RIMA
      GLOTTIDIS


•  Glottis = pair of vocal cords + pair of arytenoid cartilages.
•  Rima glottidis = the gap (plane) between them. It is what
divides the inside of the larynx into compartments.
•  The gap has two parts:
                    →
- between the 2 cords it is triangular  intermembranous
part
                      →
- between the 2 arytenoids it is four sided
intercartilaginous part
Intermembranous is the front part and the longer one.
Intercartilaginous is the short back part
•  Above the glottis = supraglottic (epiglottis side). Below the
glottis = infraglottic. Below the cricoid = trachea.

5. COMPARTMENTS OF
     THE CAVITY



•  Vestibule = between the inlet of the larynx and the false
cords.
•  Ventricle = the space between the false and true cords.
•  Supraglottic = vestibule + ventricle.
•  Infraglottic = from the true cords down to the cricoid, then
the trachea carries on.

6. THE MUSCLES


POSTERIOR CRICOARYTENOID
•  Starts on the back of the cricoid lamina (posterior surface).
•  Ends on the muscular process of the arytenoid, at the back.
•  Each arytenoid has two little bits: the vocal process at the
front (the cord is attached here) and the muscular process at
the side/back (this muscle is attached here). So pulling the
muscular process back swings the vocal process out.
• When it contracts the cords abduct, so they open and
separate. The gap widens and air goes through.
•  Only abductor of the cords.
•  Nerve: recurrent laryngeal nerve.
CRICOTHYROID
•  Attached to the cricoid (front) and the thyroid cartilage.
• When it contracts the thyroid cartilage is pulled forward
and down, so the distance between the thyroid angle and the
arytenoids gets bigger.
•  That stretches the cords and tension goes up, which
changes the pitch of the voice.
                       →
•  Nerve: external laryngeal nerve (vagus   superior
     →
laryngeal   external laryngeal).

WHAT HAPPENS IF THE NERVE IS DAMAGED
            →
•  Recurrent laryngeal   hoarseness of voice.
-  It supplies all the other intrinsic muscles apart from
cricothyroid, so the cords can't work normally.
            →
•  External laryngeal  monotonous voice.
- Cricothyroid is the one that changes pitch, so without it the
voice stays flat.

TRACHEA
   1. Anatomical Position

The trachea marks the beginning of the tracheobronchial tree.
A cylindrical tube arises at the lower border of cricoid
cartilage in the neck, as a continuation of the larynx.
Begins at the larynx (C6 level) and ends at the carina (T4-T5
level).
Bifurcation at Carina: Trachea divides into the right and left
main bronchi. Important clinically as a landmark for
bronchoscopy and respiratory pathway division.
It travels inferiorly into the superior mediastinum, bifurcating
at the level of the sternal angle (forming the right and left
main bronchi).
As it descends, the trachea is located anteriorly to the
oesophagus, and inclines slightly to the right.

2. Structure

The trachea is composed of C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings
that maintain an open airway.
The free ends of these rings are supported by the trachealis
muscle, located posteriorly, allowing flexibility and aiding in
forceful expulsion during coughing.
The trachea and bronchi are lined by ciliated pseudostratified
columnar epithelium, interspersed by goblet cells, which
produce mucus.
The combination of sweeping movements by the cilia and
mucus from the goblet cells forms the functional mucociliary
escalator.
This acts to trap inhaled particles and pathogens, moving
them up out of the airways to be swallowed and destroyed.
At the bifurcation of the primary bronchi, a ridge of cartilage
called the carina runs anteroposteriorly between the openings
of the two bronchi.
This is the most sensitive area of the trachea for triggering the
cough reflex, and can be seen on bronchoscopy.

3. Neurovascular Supply


   The trachea receives sensory innervation from the recurrent
  laryngeal nerve.
   Arterial supply comes from the tracheal branches of the
   inferior thyroid artery, while venous drainage is via the
   brachiocephalic, azygos and accessory hemiazygos veins.

  How to specifically identify bw right and left bronchiole and
  why is it imp?
  Right main bronchus is wider and shorter and is more vertical
  than the left (clinically imp: bec it is more vertical wide and
   short, usually food or small objects get stuck specifically here)
   Splits into three secondary (lobar) bronchi to supply the three
  lobes of the right lung (superior, middle, and inferior).
   Left main bronchus is longer narrower and more horizontal,
   Splits into two secondary (lobar) bronchi to supply the two
  lobes of the left lung (superior and inferior).

HISTO LAB
       (Week 4)




     OBJECTIVES

Identify different regions of the nasal cavity.
Recognize the difference between respiratory
and olfactory mucosae.
Identify the structure of the trachea.

1. Nasal cavity of mouse

Organization of cavity-
Nasal vestibule, respiratory region, olfactory region

In this histology section we shall only focus on the latter two

Respiratory region
   Largest portion of nasal cavity (2/3 rd s of it)
   Medial wall separating the cavities is smooth and is called
   nasal septum
   Lateral walls have three shelf-like structures called
   conchae, which increase surface area and cause turbulence
    in air flow





lined by respiratory mucosa consisting of –
 a) pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium- responsible
for movement of
mucous
 b) goblet cells dispersed- produce mucous
   functions to moisten inhaled air and filter it, also provides
    local immune response
   lamina propria leis just underneath and has loose
   connective tissue along with seromucous acini, blood
   vessels

Olfactory Epithelium

  occupy the upper 1/3 rd s of nasal cavity
   lined by olfactoryepithelium without goblet cells
   detect odor by specialized cells
a) olfactory receptor cells (bipolar nerve cells)- pick up on odors
b) sustentacular cells- supporting cells
  lamina propria just beneath epithelium that has bowman’s glands
   for serous watery secretions, along with connective tissue and
  blood vessels

2. L.S of human trachea

  Four visible layers of trachea
     1. Mucosa-
   Composed of respiratory epithelium and lamina propria
    2. Sub-mucosa
   Loose CT with blood vessels and seromucous acini
    3. Hyaline cartilage
   Found in the anterior region, C-shaped
    4. Adventitia
   Connects trachea to adjacent structures

 4.A) Name the circled structure.
